blocks.title: Identifying and Extending Arithmetic Sequences

discoveryHook.scenario: A runner adds 2 laps every day to her training. Day 1: 2 laps, Day 2: 4 laps, Day 3: 6 laps... The sequence of laps is arithmetic because the same number is added each day. Recognizing this constant difference lets you predict any day's distance—no guesswork needed!

explanation: A [[kw:sequence]] is an ordered list of numbers. Each number is called a [[kw:term]].
An [[kw:arithmetic sequence]] has a [[imp:constant difference]] between consecutive terms. This difference is the [[kw:common difference]], denoted by $ d $.
To find the next term, add the common difference to the previous term.
You can extend a sequence by repeatedly adding $ d $.
If the common difference is positive, the sequence increases; if negative, it decreases.

notes: $ a_{n} $ = current term, $ a_{n-1} $ = previous term.
formulaCard.title: Extending an Arithmetic Sequence

confusionCorner.body: If the terms are decreasing, the common difference is [[imp:negative]]. Always subtract a term from the next term ($ a_{n} - a_{n-1} $) to find $ d $. The sign matters!
confusionCorner.title: Common Difference Sign

questions.prompt: In an arithmetic sequence, the constant amount added to each term to get the next term is called the ___ difference.
hints: It is the same for all consecutive pairs.

questions.prompt: What is the common difference of the sequence $ 2, 5, 8, 11, \dots $?
hints: Subtract the first term from the second.

questions.prompt: Write the next term of the sequence $ 10, 7, 4, 1, \dots $.

examples.title: A – Finding the Common Difference
examples.prompt: Find the common difference of the arithmetic sequence $ 13, 18, 23, 28, \dots $ and write the next term.
steps: Subtract the first term from the second: $ 18 - 13 = 5 $.
Check: $ 23 - 18 = 5 $, $ 28 - 23 = 5 $. The common difference is $ d = 5 $.

examples.title: B – Negative Common Difference
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: How can you tell the common difference is negative, and what does that mean for the sequence?
examples.prompt: Write the next three terms of $ 60, 30, 0, -30, \dots $.
Write the next three terms of $ 1.3, 1, 0.7, 0.4, \dots $.
examples.title: C – Decimal Common Difference

teacherCues: Write the sequence 5, 10, 15, 20, ... on the board. Ask: 'What number is added each time? What would the next term be?'
Define common difference: the constant amount added to go from one term to the next.

blocks.title: Graphing Arithmetic Sequences

discoveryHook.scenario: If you graph an arithmetic sequence, the points form a perfectly straight line—just like plotting a linear function! The term's position is the x-value, and the term itself is the y-value. The common difference becomes the slope of that line.

examples.prompt: Graph the arithmetic sequence $ 4, 8, 12, 16, \dots $. What do you notice?
steps: The points lie on a straight line with slope $ 4 $.
examples.title: A – Graphing a Positive Sequence

examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why does the graph slope downward, and what does that tell you about the common difference?
examples.prompt: Graph the sequence $ 15, 12, 9, 6, \dots $. What is the slope of the line?
examples.title: B – Graphing a Decreasing Sequence
steps: Common difference $ d = -3 $, so the slope is negative.
The points fall from left to right.
The differences are not constant, so this is NOT an arithmetic sequence.
examples.title: C – Identifying a Sequence from a Graph
examples.prompt: A graph shows points $ (1,2), (2,4), (3,7), (4,11) $. Do these points represent an arithmetic sequence?

confusionCorner.title: Discrete Points, Not a Line
confusionCorner.body: Although the points of an arithmetic sequence lie on a straight line, the graph consists of [[imp:only the dots]]. You should not draw a continuous line through them because the domain is only positive integers.

teacherCues: Plot the points $ (1, 4), (2, 8), (3, 12), (4, 16) $ on a coordinate plane. Ask: 'What do you notice about these points?'
State that the points of an arithmetic sequence always lie on a straight line.

questions.prompt: When graphing an arithmetic sequence, the $ x $-coordinate of each point is the ___ number of the term.
hints: It tells where the term is in the list.
It starts at 1 for the first term.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: The x-coordinate is the position number.

hints: The slope equals the common difference.
questions.prompt: What is the slope of the line formed by the points of the sequence $ 3, 6, 9, 12, \dots $?

hints: Think of a line with negative slope.
questions.prompt: If the common difference is negative, will the graph of the sequence rise or fall from left to right?

notes: The graph is a set of discrete points, not a continuous line.
formulaCard.title: Graph of an Arithmetic Sequence
formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{Points } (n, a_n) \text{ lie on a line with slope } d $$

explanation: To graph an arithmetic sequence, let the [[imp:position number]] $ n $ be the $ x $-value and the [[imp:term]] $ a_n $ be the $ y $-value.
Plot the ordered pairs $ (n, a_n) $.
Because the difference between consecutive terms is constant, the points [[imp:lie on a straight line]].
This line has a slope equal to the common difference $ d $.
Not all points on the line belong to the sequence—only those with positive integer $ x $-values.

teacherCues: Write the formula $ a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d $ on the board. Ask: 'What does each variable represent?'
Show how to write the sequence 14, 11, 8, 5,... as $ a_n = -3n + 17 $. Emphasize that this is a linear function with domain positive integers.

questions.feedbackIfWrong: The formula uses the common difference d.
questions.prompt: The formula for the nth term of an arithmetic sequence is $ a_n = a_1 + (n-1) $ ___.
Write the simplified equation for the nth term of $ 100, 110, 120, 130, \dots $.
What is the 10th term of the sequence $ -5, -4, -3, -2, \dots $?

formulaCard.title: Equation for an Arithmetic Sequence
notes: $ a_1 $ = first term, $ d $ = common difference, $ n $ = position.

explanation: The [[imp:nth term]] of an arithmetic sequence with first term $ a_1 $ and common difference $ d $ is: $$ a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d $$
This is a linear function with slope $ d $ and $ y $-intercept $ a_1 - d $ (when written as $ a_n = dn + (a_1 - d) $).
To write an equation, identify $ a_1 $ and $ d $, substitute, and simplify.
You can use function notation: $ f(n) = a_1 + (n-1)d $. The domain is the set of positive integers.
This formula lets you find any term without listing all previous terms.

confusionCorner.title: Domain is Positive Integers
confusionCorner.body: The function $ f(n) $ for an arithmetic sequence is defined only for $ n = 1, 2, 3, \dots $. You cannot plug in $ n = 0.5 $ or negative $ n $. The graph is a set of discrete points, not a continuous line.

blocks.title: Writing Equations for Arithmetic Sequences

discoveryHook.scenario: An arithmetic sequence is like a linear function in disguise! The common difference is the slope, and the first term helps you find the y-intercept. With the formula $ a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d $, you can jump straight to any term—like finding the 50th term without listing the first 49.

confusionCorner.title: First Term vs. Initial Value
confusionCorner.body: In the carnival problem, the entry fee is $5, but the first term (for 1 game) is $7, not $5. The $5 is the $ y $-intercept of the function $ f(n) = 2n + 5 $, but the sequence starts at $ n=1 $.

examples.title: A – Online Bidding
examples.prompt: Bidding starts at $60 and increases by $5 per bid. Write a function, graph it, and find the number of bids for a winning bid of $105.
A carnival charges a $5 entry fee plus $2 per game. Write a function and find how many games you can play with $29.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why is the total cost an arithmetic sequence, and what are $ a_1 $ and $ d $?
steps: Total cost for $ n $ games: first game total $ 5+2=7 $, so $ a_1 = 7 $, $ d = 2 $.
examples.title: B – Carnival Games
C – Movie Earnings
examples.prompt: A movie earns $56 million in week 1, $48 million in week 2, $40 million in week 3. Write a function and predict earnings in week 6.

explanation: Real-life situations that increase or decrease by a fixed amount form arithmetic sequences.
The first term is the [[imp:initial value]]. The common difference is the [[imp:constant change]] per step.
Write the function as $ f(n) = a_1 + (n-1)d $ or simplify to $ f(n) = dn + b $.
Graph the sequence using discrete points (the domain is positive integers).
To answer questions, substitute the given value into the function and solve for $ n $ or evaluate $ f(n) $.

formulaCard.title: Real-Life Arithmetic Sequence Function
notes: $ a_1 $ = starting value, $ d $ = constant increase/decrease.

blocks.title: Real-Life Applications of Arithmetic Sequences

discoveryHook.scenario: From auction bidding to carnival game costs, many real-world situations grow by a constant amount each step. These are arithmetic sequences! You can model them with a linear function, graph them, and predict future values—like how many bids you can afford.

teacherCues: Pose the bidding problem: 'Online bidding increases by $5 for each bid after a $60 initial bid. How can we model this?'
Guide students to write $ f(n) = 60 + (n-1)5 $ and graph it.

hints: Look at the amount added per bid.
questions.prompt: In the bidding problem, what is the common difference?

questions.feedbackIfWrong: The $2$ is the cost per game.
hints: It's the amount added each time you play.
questions.prompt: The total cost for $ n $ carnival games is modeled by $ f(n) = 2n + 5 $. The $2$ represents the cost per ___.
Using $ f(n) = -8n + 64 $, what are the earnings in week 5?

discoveryHook.scenario: With the Understand → Solve → Conclude blueprint, you can tackle any arithmetic sequence problem. Understand the pattern (find $ a_1 $ and $ d $), Solve by writing the formula, and Conclude by finding specific terms or answering real-life questions.

examples.title: A – Full Blueprint Walkthrough

A baby boom: 5 babies born in minute 1, 10 in minute 2, 15 in minute 3. Write a function and predict minutes for 100 babies.

steps: Solve: Points $ (1,4), (2,2), (3,0), (4,-2) $. Plot as discrete dots.
Conclude: The graph falls from left to right; the common difference is negative.

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid – Working with Arithmetic Sequences

rows.1: 50th term: $ a_{50} = -133 $. Sequence decreases by 3 each step.

explanation: The blueprint for arithmetic sequences: [[imp:Understand]] – Determine if the sequence is arithmetic by checking for a constant difference. Identify $ a_1 $ and $ d $.
[[imp:Solve]] – Write the nth term formula $ a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d $ or function $ f(n) = a_1 + (n-1)d $. Simplify if needed. Graph the sequence as discrete points.
[[imp:Conclude]] – Use the formula to find any term, answer real-life questions, or predict future values. State whether the graph is rising (positive $ d $) or falling (negative $ d $).

confusionCorner.title: Arithmetic Check
confusionCorner.body: Always verify that the difference is constant for at least three pairs. A sequence like $ 1, 2, 4, 8 $ has differences $ 1, 2, 4 $ — not constant — so it is [[imp:not arithmetic]].

teacherCues: Display the Understand → Solve → Conclude framework. Walk through a sequence problem: identify first term and common difference, write the formula, use it.
Emphasize: 'Understand' identifies whether the sequence is arithmetic by checking for a constant difference.

hints: They are the parameters in the formula.
One is the starting term, the other is the constant change.
questions.prompt: In the blueprint, what two things must you identify in the Understand phase?
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Identify the first term $ a_1 $ and the common difference $ d $.

questions.prompt: If a sequence has constant differences, it is an ___ sequence.
hints: It's the topic of this lesson.

title: Chapter 4.6 — Arithmetic Sequences
presenterNotes: Emphasize the connection between arithmetic sequences and linear functions: the common difference is the slope, and the points lie on a line.
When graphing, students often want to connect the dots. Remind them that the domain is discrete (positive integers), so only the points are part of the sequence.
For the formula $ a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d $, many students mistakenly use $ n $ instead of $ n-1 $. Use the table method to show why the first term has no $ d $ added.
Real-life problems are a good opportunity to reinforce function notation and the concept of domain restrictions.
